The Mackerel icefish Champsocephalus gunnari, a notothenioid endemic to the Southern Ocean, attains a maximum recorded standard length of 66 centimeters [Li = 66 centimeters], a value that distinguishes it as one of the larger-bodied species within the channichthyid family. Field surveys conducted around South Georgia indicate that this ultimate length is reached after several years of sustained somatic growth in the cold, productive waters of the Antarctic shelf. The standard length at which sexual maturation is initiated has been documented at 26.2 centimeters [Lp = 26.2 centimeters]. This reproductive milestone marks the transition from the juvenile growth phase to the reproductively active adult stage, a shift that occurs relatively early in the species' ontogeny given its substantial asymptotic size. Individuals that have attained this length have typically undergone the full process of gonadal recrudescence and are physiologically capable of participating in spawning aggregations. The relationship between body size and reproductive readiness has been corroborated by histological examination of ovarian tissue from specimens collected during the austral summer.

The wet weight at which individuals typically attain sexual maturity has been estimated at 97.7 grams [Wwp = 97.7 grams], a body mass that corresponds closely to the aforementioned length-based threshold and that reflects the energetic reserves necessary for gonad development. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum body mass achieved by adults in natural populations, is considerably greater at approximately 2400 grams [Wwi = approximately 2400 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to the largest specimens encountered in trawl surveys. This substantial increase in mass from the pubertal stage to the asymptotic size highlights the capacity for continued somatic investment even after the onset of reproductive activity. The species' body plan, characterized by a reduced number of erythrocytes and a low-density skeletal structure, contributes to a relatively low overall body density, an adaptation to the pelagic lifestyle that these fish maintain throughout their life cycle.

At the commencement of its life cycle, the Mackerel icefish emerges from the egg as a yolk-sac larva weighing approximately 0.031 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.031 grams]. This neonatal mass is based on the dimensions of the demersal egg, which typically measures between 3.5 and 4.1 millimeters in diameter, and the larval body that develops within the chorion during the incubation period. The incubation process itself is strongly temperature-dependent, and under the prevailing thermal regime of 1.5 °C [T = 1.5 °C] that characterizes the benthic spawning grounds, embryogenesis is completed in approximately 95 days [ab = approximately 95 days]. This protracted period of yolk-dependent development is typical of high-latitude Antarctic fishes, where metabolic rates are suppressed by the chronically cold environment, allowing for slow, efficient utilization of the endogenous yolk reserves. Following eclosion, the prolarva remains non-feeding for a brief period as it absorbs the remainder of its yolk sac.

The complete life cycle under the ambient thermal conditions of 1.5 °C [T = 1.5 °C] spans approximately 5475 days [am = approximately 5475 days], representing a maximum longevity of roughly 15 years for this Antarctic species. This extended lifespan, which is considerable for a teleost of its body size, reflects the slow pace of life characteristic of high-latitude notothenioids, whose physiological processes are constrained by low temperatures and pronounced seasonal fluctuations in food availability. Over the course of this long reproductive life, females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate that has been documented under the same thermal conditions of 1.5 °C [T = 1.5 °C]. Females produce approximately 32 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 32 eggs per spawning event], and given that a single spawning is completed each year [F_R_i = single spawning is completed each year], the total annual fecundity reflects this relatively modest clutch size when compared to other demersal-spawning notothenioids that broadcast larger numbers of smaller pelagic eggs.

The seasonal timing of the spawning event is tightly coupled to the austral winter, with peak gamete release occurring between May and June when water temperatures are at their minimum. Following fertilisation, the demersal eggs adhere to the substrate in discrete clusters, where they are subject to the cold but stable thermal conditions of the deep shelf environment. The extended incubation period of approximately three months at 1.5 °C [T = 1.5 °C], as previously noted, ensures that hatching coincides with the spring phytoplankton bloom, thereby maximising prey availability for the newly emerged yolk-sac larvae. This temporal alignment between the age at birth of 95 days [ab = 95 days] and the seasonal production of zooplankton is a critical determinant of early larval survival at a temperature of 1.5 °C [T = 1.5 °C]. The slow pace of embryonic development is counterbalanced by the production of relatively large, well-provisioned eggs that yield larvae with substantial endogenous energy stores, allowing them to withstand brief periods of food scarcity before the onset of exogenous feeding.
